questions.q: What is the name of this ester?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of an ester: a three-carbon acyl part, C=O at its end, joined through a single-bonded oxygen to a two-carbon alkyl group.

questions.solution: An ester is named alkyl alkanoate. The alkyl group is the part joined to the single-bonded oxygen, from the alcohol: here two carbons, ethyl. The acid part includes the C=O carbon: here three carbons, propanoate. So it is ethyl propanoate. (Reading the parts the wrong way round leads to propyl ethanoate, an isomer.)

questions.q: Propanoic acid reacts with sodium carbonate solution. Which products form?

options.C: Propanal, carbon dioxide and sodium hydroxide
options.D: Sodium propanoate, carbon dioxide and water

questions.solution: A carboxylic acid reacts with a carbonate like any acid, giving a salt, carbon dioxide and water: \(\mathrm{2CH_{3}CH_{2}COOH + Na_{2}CO_{3} \rightarrow 2CH_{3}CH_{2}COONa + CO_{2} + H_{2}O}\). The fizzing is the test for a carboxylic acid. (Hydrogen forms with a reactive metal, not a carbonate.)

questions.q: Which conditions are used to make an ester from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol?

options.A: Warm with a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid as a catalyst
options.B: Heat under reflux with aqueous sodium hydroxide
options.C: Mix at room temperature with no catalyst

questions.solution: Esterification is slow and reversible: \(\mathrm{RCOOH + R'OH \rightleftharpoons RCOOR' + H_{2}O}\). A strong acid catalyst, concentrated sulfuric acid, and warming speed it up. (Sodium hydroxide hydrolyses esters, the reverse process.)

questions.q: Methyl butanoate is heated under reflux with sodium hydroxide solution. Which products form?
questions.solution: Alkaline hydrolysis breaks the ester at the C–O single bond, giving the alcohol and the salt of the acid: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}COOCH_{3} + NaOH \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}COONa + CH_{3}OH}\). (Butanoic acid and methanol are the products of acid hydrolysis; in alkali the acid is turned into its salt.)

questions.q: Why does the alkaline hydrolysis of an ester go to completion, whereas acid hydrolysis does not?

options.A: Hydroxide ions are a catalyst, but hydrogen ions are not
options.B: The carboxylate ion formed in alkali cannot react with the alcohol to re-form the ester
options.C: Alkaline hydrolysis is carried out at a higher temperature
options.D: The alcohol formed in alkali evaporates from the mixture

questions.solution: Acid hydrolysis is the reverse of esterification and reaches an equilibrium. In alkali the carboxylic acid formed is deprotonated to a carboxylate ion, which cannot react with the alcohol, so the reverse reaction stops and the hydrolysis goes to completion. (Hydroxide ions are used up, so they are a reactant, not a catalyst.)

questions.q: Ethanoic acid (\(M_{\text{r}} = 60\)) boils at 118 °C and propan-1-ol (\(M_{\text{r}} = 60\)) at 97 °C. Why does ethanoic acid boil higher?

options.A: Ethanoic acid has stronger London forces because it has more electrons
options.B: Only ethanoic acid forms hydrogen bonds
options.C: Ethanoic acid molecules ionise in the liquid, forming ionic bonds
options.D: Ethanoic acid molecules form more hydrogen bonds, pairing up as dimers

questions.solution: Both compounds hydrogen bond. Ethanoic acid has both an O–H hydrogen and a C=O oxygen, so two molecules can join through two hydrogen bonds as a dimer, and more energy is needed to separate them. (Propan-1-ol also hydrogen bonds, through its O–H group.)

questions.q: Propanenitrile is heated under reflux with dilute hydrochloric acid. What are the products?
questions.solution: Acid hydrolysis turns the nitrile group into a carboxylic acid group, keeping all the carbons: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CN + 2H_{2}O + HCl \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}COOH + NH_{4}Cl}\). The nitrogen ends up as ammonium chloride. (The CN carbon becomes the COOH carbon, so the acid still has three carbons.)

questions.q: Ethanoic acid is reduced by \(\mathrm{LiAlH_{4}}\) in dry ether. What is the organic product?
questions.solution: \(\mathrm{LiAlH_{4}}\) reduces carboxylic acids all the way to primary alcohols: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH + 4[H] \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}OH + H_{2}O}\). Any aldehyde formed on the way is reduced faster than the acid, so it cannot be isolated. (\(\mathrm{NaBH_{4}}\) does not reduce carboxylic acids.)

questions.q: Which reagent carries out this conversion at room temperature?

figure.alt: Reaction scheme: ethanoic acid is converted into ethanoyl chloride, CH3COCl. A question mark stands over the arrow in place of the reagent.

questions.solution: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH + PCl_{5} \rightarrow CH_{3}COCl + POCl_{3} + HCl}\). Phosphorus(V) chloride replaces the OH group with Cl, and steamy fumes of hydrogen chloride are seen. (Chlorine in UV light substitutes hydrogen atoms on the methyl group, not the OH.)

questions.q: Ethanoyl chloride is added to ethanol at room temperature. Which products form?
questions.solution: The ethanol oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon and chloride is eliminated: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCl + CH_{3}CH_{2}OH \rightarrow CH_{3}COOCH_{2}CH_{3} + HCl}\). Unlike esterification from the acid, this is fast, not reversible, and gives HCl, not water. (Ethanoic acid and HCl are the products with water.)

questions.q: Ethanoyl chloride reacts with methylamine, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}NH_{2}}\). What is the organic product other than the methylammonium salt?
questions.solution: The nitrogen lone pair of methylamine attacks the carbonyl carbon, and chloride and an H on the nitrogen are lost: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCl + 2CH_{3}NH_{2} \rightarrow CH_{3}CONHCH_{3} + CH_{3}NH_{3}^{+}Cl^{-}}\). The product is an N-substituted amide, N-methylethanamide. (Ethanamide is the product with ammonia.)

questions.q: What is the name of this type of mechanism?

figure.alt: Mechanism diagram: ethanoyl chloride and a water molecule. A curly arrow goes from a lone pair on the water oxygen to the δ+ carbonyl carbon, and the C=O bond pair moves onto the oxygen. In the intermediate the C=O re-forms, a chloride ion leaves, and an H+ is lost, giving ethanoic acid.

questions.solution: Water, a nucleophile, first adds to the δ+ carbonyl carbon as the C=O bond opens. The C=O bond then re-forms and a chloride ion is eliminated, with loss of H+. Addition followed by elimination makes it nucleophilic addition–elimination. (The overall change looks like substitution, but the mechanism goes through an addition intermediate.)

questions.q: Aspirin can be made using either ethanoic anhydride or ethanoyl chloride. Why does industry use ethanoic anhydride?

options.A: It gives a higher atom economy
options.B: It is cheaper, less corrosive and reacts less violently, and it does not give off hydrogen chloride
options.C: It reacts much faster than ethanoyl chloride
options.D: It is the only one that gives the ester group in aspirin

questions.solution: Ethanoic anhydride is cheaper, less corrosive and less vulnerable to hydrolysis by moisture, and its by-product is ethanoic acid rather than corrosive hydrogen chloride gas. Its reaction is slower and easier to control. (Its by-product, ethanoic acid, is heavier than HCl, so the atom economy is lower, not higher.)

questions.q: Biodiesel is made from vegetable oils, such as palm oil. Which substance is the oil reacted with, and what is the other product?
questions.solution: Vegetable oils are triesters of propane-1,2,3-triol. Reacting them with methanol, with a catalyst, swaps the glycerol for methyl groups: \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{5}(OOCR)_{3} + 3CH_{3}OH \rightarrow 3RCOOCH_{3} + C_{3}H_{5}(OH)_{3}}\). Biodiesel is the mixture of methyl esters. (Sodium hydroxide gives soap, a different product.)

questions.q: Shea butter, a fat, is heated with sodium hydroxide solution to make soap. Which products form?

options.A: Methyl esters of long-chain carboxylic acids, and propane-1,2,3-triol
options.C: Sodium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids, and propane-1,2,3-triol

questions.solution: A fat is a triester of propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol) with long-chain carboxylic acids. Alkaline hydrolysis breaks the three ester groups, giving glycerol and the sodium salts of the acids, which are soap. (Methyl esters form with methanol: that is biodiesel.)

questions.q: 6.00 g of ethanoic acid (\(M_{\text{r}} = 60.0\)) is heated with excess ethanol and a sulfuric acid catalyst. 4.84 g of ethyl ethanoate (\(M_{\text{r}} = 88.0\)) is collected. What is the percentage yield?
questions.solution: Moles of ethanoic acid = \(\frac{6.00}{60.0}\) = 0.100 mol, so the maximum mass of ester = 0.100 × 88.0 = 8.80 g. Percentage yield = \(\frac{4.84}{8.80} \times 100\) = 55.0%. (Comparing the 4.84 g of ester with the 6.00 g of acid leads to 80.7%.)
